jp2a
====

jp2a is a simple JPEG to ASCII converter.

The source is available at <https://github.com/cslarsen/jp2a>. This project
used to be hosted on SourceForge.

License
-------

Copyright 2006-2016 Christian Stigen Larsen  
Distributed under the GNU General Public License v2.

You can read the full license in the file COPYING. jp2a also uses other
libraries. These licenses can be found in the file LICENSES.

Usage
-----

jp2a converts JPEG images to ASCII characters. You can specify a mixture of 
files and URLs.

**Basic usage:**

```
jp2a [options] [filename(s) | URL(s)]
```

**Common options:**

- `-` - Read JPEG image from standard input
- `--size=WIDTHxHEIGHT` - Set output dimensions
- `--width=N` - Set output width (height calculated automatically)
- `--height=N` - Set output height (width calculated automatically)
- `--chars=...` - Use specific characters for output (default: "   ...',;:clodxkO0KXNWM")
- `--invert` or `-i` - Invert output image
- `--background=light` or `--background=dark` - Set background type
- `--border` or `-b` - Frame output in a border
- `--colors` - Use ANSI color for text output and CSS color for HTML output
- `--html` - Output in XHTML 1.0 format
- `--output=FILE` - Write output to file
- `--term-fit` or `-f` - Fit image to terminal display
- `--flipx` or `-x` - Flip output horizontally
- `--flipy` or `-y` - Flip output vertically
- `--help` or `-h` - Display help
- `--version` or `-V` - Print version

Examples
--------

Convert and print a JPEG file:

```
jp2a imagefile.jpg
```

Convert with specific dimensions:

```
jp2a --size=40x20 imagefile.jpg
```

Download an image from the web and convert:

```
jp2a http://example.com/image.jpg
```

Use specific characters for output:

```
jp2a --chars=" ...ooxx@@" picture.jpg
```

Read from standard input:

```
cat image.jpg | jp2a --width=76 -
```

Use with ImageMagick to convert other image formats:

```
convert somefile.png jpg:- | jp2a - --width=80
```

Output to HTML:

```
jp2a --html --output=output.html image.jpg
```

For more detailed information, see the man page: `man jp2a`

.B \-i \-\-invert
Invert output image.  If you view a picture with white background, but you are using
a display with light characters on a dark background, you shoudl invert the image.
.TP
.BI \-\-red= ...
.TP
.BI \-\-green= ...
.TP
.BI \-\-blue= ...
When converting from RGB to grayscale, use the given weights to calculate luminance.
These three floating point values must add up to exactly 1.0.
The default is red=0.2989, green=0.5866 and blue=0.1145.
.TP
.BI \-\-size= WIDTHxHEIGHT
Set output dimension.
.TP
.B \-v \-\-verbose
Print some verbose information to standard error when reading each JPEG image.
.TP
.BI \-\-width= N
Set output width.  If you only specify the width, the height will be
calculated automatically.
.TP
.B \-V \-\-version
Print program version.
.TP
.B \-\-zoom
Sets output dimensions to your entire terminal window, disregarding source image
aspect ratio.
.SH RETURN VALUES
jp2a returns 1 when errors are encountered, zero for no errors.
.SH EXAMPLES
Convert and print imagefile.jpg using ASCII characters in 40 columns and 20 rows:
.PP
.B jp2a
\-\-size=40x20 imagefile.jpg
.PP
Download an image off the net, convert and print:
.PP
.B jp2a
http://www.google.com/intl/en/logos/easter_logo.jpg
.PP
Output picture.jpg and picture2.jpg, each 80x25 characters, using the characters " ...ooxx@@" for output:
.PP
.B jp2a
\-\-size=80x25 --chars=" ...ooxx@@" picture.jpg picture2.jpg
.PP
Output image.jpg using 76 columns, height is automatically calculated from aspect ratio of image.jpg
.PP
cat image.jpg |
.B jp2a
\-\-width=76 \-
.PP
If you use jp2a together with ImageMagick's convert(1) then you can make good use of pipes,
and have ImageMagick do all sorts of image conversions and effects on the source image.  For example:
.PP
.B convert
somefile.png jpg:\- |
.B jp2a
\- \-\-width=80
.PP
Check out convert(1) options to see what you can do.  Convert can handle almost any image format,
so with this combination you can convert images in e.g. PDF or AVI files to ASCII.
.PP
Although the default build of jp2a includes automatic downloading of files specified by URLs,
you can explicitly download them by using curl(1) or wget(1), for example:
.PP
.B curl
\-s
http://foo.bar/image.jpg |
.B convert
\- jpg:- |
.B jp2a
\-
.SH DOWNLOADING IMAGES FROM THE NET
If you have compiled jp2a with libcurl(3), you can download images by specifying URLs:

.B jp2a
https://user:pass@foo.com/bar.jpg

The protocols recognized are ftp, ftps, file, http, https and tftp.

If you need more control of the downloading, you should use curl(1) or wget(1) and jp2a
read the image from standard input.

jp2a uses pipe and fork to download images using libcurl (i.e., no exec or system calls) 
and therefore does not worry about malevolently formatted URLs.
.SH GRAYSCALE CONVERSION
You can extract the red channel by doing this:

.B jp2a
somefile.jpg --red=1.0 --green=0.0 --blue=0.0

This will calculate luminance based on Y = R*1.0 + G*0.0 + B*0.0.  The default
values is to use Y = R*0.2989 + G*0.5866 + B*0.1145.
.SH PROJECT HOMEPAGE
The latest version of jp2a and news is always available from https://github.com/cslarsen/jp2a
.SH SEE ALSO
cjpeg(1), djpeg(1), jpegtran(1), convert(1)
.SH BUGS
jp2a does not interpolate when resizing.  If you want better quality, try using convert(1)
and convert the source image to the exact output dimensions before using jp2a.
.PP
Another issue is that jp2a skips some X-pixels along each scanline.  This gives a less
precise output image, and will probably be corrected in future versions.

Christian Stigen Larsen

jp2a uses jpeglib to read JPEG files.  jpeglib is made by The Independent JPEG Group (IJG),
who have a page at http://www.ijg.org

    r = subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, capture_output=True, **kw)

def run(args, env=None, stdin_data=None):

def patch_height(src, dst, new_h):
    d=bytearray(open(src,'rb').read())
    # Find SOF0 marker FFC0
    for i in range(len(d)-10):
        if d[i]==0xFF and d[i+1]==0xC0:
            # SOF length at i+2,i+3
            # height at i+5,i+6
            old=(d[i+5]<<8|d[i+6])
            print(f"found SOF at {i}, old height {old}")
            d[i+5]=(new_h>>8)&0xFF
            d[i+6]=new_h&0xFF
            open(dst,'wb').write(d)
            print(f"patched to {new_h}, wrote {dst} len {len(d)}")
            return
    print("not found")

    def write(self, code, length):
        self.acc=(self.acc<<length)|code

        while self.nbits>=8:

    import subprocess as sp

    return r

# Create gradient 32x8

write_jpeg_grayscale(w,h,pix,[8]*64,"/tmp/grad32.jpg")

out=r.stdout.decode().splitlines()
print(out)
# out should be 16x? height? 16*8/32*0.5=2 => 2 rows
for line in out:
    idxs=[pal23.index(c) for c in line]
    print(idxs)
    # compute expected source values for each sampling hypothesis
    # hypothesis A: src_x = x * SW / W = x*2
    # hypothesis B: src_x = (x+0.5)*SW/W -0.5? (center)
    # hypothesis C: average of 2 pixels?
    vals=[int(x*255/(w-1)) for x in range(w)]
    print("  src vals", vals)
    for i,ch in enumerate(line):
        # hypothesis A src
        sx_a=i*2
        v_a=vals[sx_a]
        exp_a=(v_a*22+127)//255
        # hypothesis avg of 2
        v_avg=(vals[sx_a]+vals[sx_a+1])//2 if sx_a+1<w else vals[sx_a]
        exp_avg=(v_avg*22+127)//255
        print(f"  i={i} actual={pal23.index(ch)} expA={exp_a}(v={v_a}) expAvg={exp_avg}(v={v_avg})")
    print()

            # assume 1 table

            # print("qtable", qtable[:8])
            pass
        elif m==0xC0:
            height=(d[pos+3]<<8|d[pos+4])
            width=(d[pos+5]<<8|d[pos+6])
            print(f"SOF {width}x{height}")
        elif m==0xC4:
            # DHT - may contain multiple tables in one segment? Our encoder writes separate segments, but logo writes combined? Need to handle.
            # Parse all tables in segment
            end=pos+ln
            p=pos+2
            while p < end:

                bits=[0]+list(d[p:p+16]); p+=16
                total=sum(bits[1:])
                vals=list(d[p:p+total]); p+=total

            # Find EOI

            scan_end=len(d)-2
            scan=d[scan_start:scan_end]
            print(f" scan len {len(scan)}")
            return width,height,qtable,huff_dc,huff_ac,scan
        pos+=ln
    return None

    return r

    r=run(["--width=4","--html","--colors","--fill",f"--background={bg}","assets/grind.jpg"])

# ANSI fill with light vs dark? Does background affect ANSI?

    r=run(["--width=4","--colors","--fill",f"--background={bg}","assets/grind.jpg"])

    r=run(["--width=4","--html",f"--background={bg}","assets/grind.jpg"])

jp2a
====

jp2a is a simple JPEG to ASCII converter.

The source is available at <https://github.com/cslarsen/jp2a>. This project
used to be hosted on SourceForge.

License
-------

Copyright 2006-2016 Christian Stigen Larsen  
Distributed under the GNU General Public License v2.

You can read the full license in the file COPYING. jp2a also uses other
libraries. These licenses can be found in the file LICENSES.

Usage
-----

jp2a converts JPEG images to ASCII characters. You can specify a mixture of 
files and URLs.

**Basic usage:**

```
jp2a [options] [filename(s) | URL(s)]
```

**Common options:**

- `-` - Read JPEG image from standard input
- `--size=WIDTHxHEIGHT` - Set output dimensions
- `--width=N` - Set output width (height calculated automatically)
- `--height=N` - Set output height (width calculated automatically)
- `--chars=...` - Use specific characters for output (default: "   ...',;:clodxkO0KXNWM")
- `--invert` or `-i` - Invert output image
- `--background=light` or `--background=dark` - Set background type
- `--border` or `-b` - Frame output in a border
- `--colors` - Use ANSI color for text output and CSS color for HTML output
- `--html` - Output in XHTML 1.0 format
- `--output=FILE` - Write output to file
- `--term-fit` or `-f` - Fit image to terminal display
- `--flipx` or `-x` - Flip output horizontally
- `--flipy` or `-y` - Flip output vertically
- `--help` or `-h` - Display help
- `--version` or `-V` - Print version

Examples
--------

def get_bars(img, width):
    import subprocess as sp
    r=sp.run(["./executable","-v",f"--width={width}",img], capture_output=True)

import struct
def bars_single(y,h):
    # C float: (y+2)*54.0f/h +0.5f then (int)
    x = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', (y+2)*54.0/h + 0.5))[0]
    # Actually (y+2)*54.0f/h computed in float: (y+2) int to float, *54.0f (float), /h (int to float) -> float, +0.5f -> float, then (int) truncation
    # In Python, (y+2)*54/h with ints gives float double, then +0.5 double, then int. To mimic float, convert intermediate to single?
    # Steps: a = float32(y+2), b = float32(54.0), c = a*b (float32), d = float32(h), e = c/d (float32), f = e + float32(0.5), bars = int(f) (truncation, with float32 value)
    a = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', float(y+2)))[0]
    b = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', 54.0))[0]
    c = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', a*b))[0]
    d = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', float(h)))[0]
    e = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', c/d))[0]
    f = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('f', e+0.5))[0]
    return int(f)
    # Actually int(f) for positive truncates toward zero, same as C (int) cast (which truncates). Good.
